newsitem.title: USA: Montgomery Ward stops paying suppliers.
newsitem.headline: Montgomery Ward stops paying suppliers.

text.p: Ailing retailer Montgomery Ward Holding Corp. has stopped paying some of its vendors, a sign the company's financial woes are building, sources said Wednesday.
Some factoring companies, which fund receivables for vendors to retailers, said Ward has not paid for goods that were shipped late last month.
The privately held retailer has told vendors that payments will begin flowing in a couple of days, sources said. But suppliers were expected to delay or halt fresh shipments to avoid further risk.

"I think a lot of suppliers will try to stop goods that are in transit," said Charles Johnson, executive vice president of Heller Financial Inc., a financial services company. "It could affect Montgomery Ward right away. If goods are not flowing, there won't be new merchandise for sale."
Ward's decision to stop payments likely stemmed from disagreement between the company and its lenders over the retailer's near-term business strategy, analysts said.

The company is negotiating with lenders to postpone a payment deadline for $1.4 billion in debt. It also is seeking to close a deal to sell its Signature Group direct marketing unit, and the company has said it is pleased with the progress of those talks.
But a dispute apparently has erupted between Ward, its lenders and General Electric Co.'s GE Capital unit, which owns half of the company, over how to use proceeds of the Signature sale.

"The vendors pulling credit really is a symptom. It's not the problem," said Barry Bryant of Rodman & Renshaw Inc. "I think what's going on here is a fight between GE Capital and the banks over who is going to get the most out of this company."
Until Signature is sold, Ward will have difficulty arranging a new financing package that would give it liquidity and breathing room to make it through the fall and holiday seasons, analysts said.

Ward has said it has not ruled out the possibility of seeking Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection from creditors. Some experts said Ward could have decided to stop paying bills to build a war chest that could be protected from suppliers and be used to buy new goods if it were to file for bankruptcy.
On the other hand, Ward has been mapping a strategy to turn around its sagging retail business.
On Tuesday, it said it would remodel four to six stores early next year and focus on its core appliance and furniture businesses to boost sales. Last year, Montgomery Ward lost $249 million.
